builder_plan.scenario: Your self-hosted model spends too long generating answers token by token.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a compatible draft model and serving integration exist before renting compute.
builder_plan.baseline: The same target with speculation off, then your existing drafter if you have one.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted draft length, tokens per second, tail latency, output quality, and total GPU cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
summary: The method replaces the strong model's per-step autoregressive generation of agent tool-call trajectories with a weak model drafting grounded multi-step segments that the strong model verifies in a single parallel prefill pass, committing the longest valid prefix and repairing the first rejected step. It costs implementation complexity (a draft-verify-repair protocol, read-only tool gating, and semantic verification logic) plus the latency of verification passes and occasional repair decoding, with a small residual quality gap relative to the strong model alone. It can fail when the weak model drafts trajectories that are semantically plausible but subtly wrong, when verification accepts invalid steps because prefix-level review misses cross-step errors, or when repair rates rise on hard tasks and erode the latency savings.
rationale: The protocol is implementable on a single GPU or via APIs without model training and directly reduces cost and latency in tool-using agents, but its gains depend on the weak-strong model pair and task mix, so it requires validation on the reader's own agent workload before production adoption.
technique: Trajectory-level speculative drafting with strong-model verification

claims.statement: The method replaces the strong model's per-step autoregressive generation of agent tool-call trajectories with a weak model drafting grounded multi-step segments that the strong model verifies in a single parallel prefill pass, committing the longest valid prefix and repairing the first rejected step. It costs implementation complexity (a draft-verify-repair protocol, read-only tool gating, and semantic verification logic) plus the latency of verification passes and occasional repair decoding, with a small residual quality gap relative to the strong model alone. It can fail when the weak model drafts trajectories that are semantically plausible but subtly wrong, when verification accepts invalid steps because prefix-level review misses cross-step errors, or when repair rates rise on hard tasks and erode the latency savings.

On tau^2-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time; on other benchmarks it recovers 44-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens.
